title: The night before the summit
hookLine: like the night under the tree: sit, and don't hurry
tomorrow: five years of mornings. who actually walked them?

cards: The night before something big has its own sound: the fridge humming, a car passing, and a mind that wants to get up and fix one more thing. Check the email again. Redo the list.
Mai is having that night right now. The Buddha's biggest night, in the tradition's telling, began with a promise not to get up.
Tradition says he spread grass under the bodhi tree, sat facing east, and resolved: let my skin and sinews and bones dry up, I will not rise from this seat until I wake up.

teach.b: Then the night went on, and the Buddha tells it in his own voice, in the Majjhima Nikaya. First his mind grew still, there in the seat, quiet and clear.
Then, one watch at a time: in the first watch of the night he remembered his past lives.

teach.h: THE MIDDLE WATCH: BEINGS AND ACTIONS.
teach.b: In the middle watch he saw beings die and arise according to their actions.

teach.h: THE LAST WATCH: THE FOUR TRUTHS.
teach.b: In the last watch he saw dukkha, its arising, its ending and the way, and ignorance gave way to knowledge, as it does, he says, for one who stays diligent and resolute. Three watches, and no leaving the seat between them.
Later tellings remember Mara's storms that night, and a hand on the earth. The sutta puts something plainer at the center: not a battle, a long sit.
The Dhammapada keeps lines tradition places at that dawn, in Max Müller's words: "maker of the tabernacle, thou hast been seen; thou shalt not make up this tabernacle again."
Tradition reads the maker as craving, the builder of the house, putting it up again and again. Once the builder is seen, the building stops.
In this telling, awakening didn't come from running anywhere, or from fixing one more thing. It came in one seat, watch by watch, until morning.
Stay put. Let the night do its work.

how: Buddhists remember the night of awakening in sitting practice and at festivals such as Vesak or Bodhi Day, when some sit through the night; Buddha images with one hand touching the earth recall the same night.

games.q: what does “the night before the summit” mean?
o: the night the Buddha left his palace to start his search
a fast before ordination, kept by monks for a whole night
the night of awakening under the tree, sat through to dawn

games.q: the night under the tree — tap the pairs.
p: he saw beings arise by their actions
he saw the four truths; ignorance gave way
i will not rise from this seat

s: in the Majjhima Nikaya, the Buddha tells his awakening as one moment, with no stages
he tells it in stages: first a still mind, then three watches, through the whole night.
in the sutta's own telling, the night is mostly a battle with Mara
the Majjhima Nikaya tells it as three watches of sitting; Mara's storms come from later tellings.
Dhammapada 154 speaks to a 'maker of the tabernacle'
in Max Müller's words; tradition reads the maker as craving, the builder of the house.

games.q: a friend new to meditation says she'll start sitting 'once my mind is calm enough.' what does the night under the tree suggest?
o: sit now, restless mind and all; he stayed in his seat through the whole night.
wait for a calm day; awakening only comes once the mind is already quiet.
think the restless thoughts through first, then sit once they're all solved.
games.why: in the sutta the stillness came in the seat: he sat, his mind settled, and the three watches followed. the calm grew from sitting; it wasn't the ticket in.

practice: If it's night where you are, turn off one light. Sit, close your eyes, and divide the sit into three short watches: a first, a middle, a last. Hurry nothing.
Each time the mind wants to get up and fix something, notice the pull, and stay in your seat until the next watch comes round.

wordCard.voice: The night before the summit: the night under the tree, three watches long, sat through without getting up.

orig.note: Pali: gahakaraka, house-builder; the maker in Dhammapada 154.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: stay put, the way he did, one watch at a time. Thirteen days up; one to go.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 36 (Mahasaccaka Sutta) and Majjhima Nikaya 4: the three knowledges in the three watches of the night
Nidanakatha (introduction to the Jataka): the seat under the tree, the resolve, Mara and the earth witness
